the copied entry. Pass src and dst VMAs consistently instead of src and
dst MM. Move the TODO.
title: mm/huge_memory: properly handle refcounted PUD mappings on fork

desc:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

hwmon: (coretemp) Set nr_cores only after core_data allocation succeeds

In init_temp_data(), pdata->nr_cores is populated from
topology_num_cores_per_package() before allocating pdata->core_data. If
that allocation fails, init_temp_data() returns NULL with
pdata->core_data still NULL and pdata->nr_cores set to a positive value.

coretemp_add_core() logs the error without failing coretemp_cpu_online(),
so the CPU still comes online with pdata->hwmon_dev registered. When the
CPU is later taken offline (or the module is unloaded),
coretemp_cpu_offline() calls get_temp_data(pd, cpu), which loops up to
pdata->nr_cores and dereferences the NULL pdata->core_data pointer.

Store the core count in a local variable and assign pdata->nr_cores only
after pdata->core_data is allocated, preserving the invariant that
pdata->nr_cores is zero whenever pdata->core_data is NULL.
title: hwmon: (coretemp) Set nr_cores only after core_data allocation succeeds

desc:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

hwmon: (pmbus/q54sj108a2) Add missing NULL pointer check

When CONFIG_DEBUG_FS is enabled and per-client PMBus debugfs directory
creation fails during pmbus_do_probe(), q54sj108a2_probe() passes the NULL
pointer returned by pmbus_get_debugfs_dir() to debugfs_create_dir()
without validation, creating its debugfs directory at the debugfs root
instead of under the client directory.

If pmbus_init_debugfs() fails to create the client directory, data->debugfs
is left as NULL or an ERR_PTR, which pmbus_get_debugfs_dir() converts to
NULL. Passing a NULL parent to debugfs_create_dir() places q54sj108a2_dir
in the root of the debugfs filesystem and populates it with attribute files
whose private data pointers reference psu->debugfs_entries. Because this
root-level directory is outside the client debugfs hierarchy, PMBus core
cleanup does not remove it on device unbind, leaking the debugfs entries
and causing a use-after-free of the devm-allocated struct q54sj108a2_data
if the orphaned files are accessed via q54sj108a2_debugfs_read() or
q54sj108a2_debugfs_write() after device removal.

Fix the problem by adding the missing NULL pointer check.
title: hwmon: (pmbus/q54sj108a2) Add missing NULL pointer check

desc:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

hwmon: (peci/dimmtemp) Fix devres leak and UAF on concurrent unbind

When a peci_dimmtemp device is unbound concurrently with its delayed
initialization work (detect_work), newly allocated devm resources and
the hwmon device are leaked, leading to a use-after-free when reading
the lingering hwmon sysfs attributes.

In peci_dimmtemp_probe(), detect_work is registered for cancellation via
devm_delayed_work_autocancel(). During driver detach, devres_release_all()
first moves all existing entries from dev->devres_head onto a local todo
list before invoking their release callbacks in reverse order. If
create_dimm_temp_info_delayed() is already running when
devm_delayed_work_drop() calls cancel_delayed_work_sync(),
create_dimm_temp_info() can allocate dimmtemp_label strings via
devm_kzalloc()/devm_kasprintf() and register the hwmon device via
devm_hwmon_device_register_with_info(), appending new devres entries to
the now-empty dev->devres_head. Once the work finishes,
devres_release_all() frees priv and priv->name from the local todo list
without re-evaluating dev->devres_head, leaving the late devres
allocations and registered hwmon device behind with a dangling priv
pointer.

Cancel detect_work synchronously in a driver .remove() callback instead
of relying on devm_delayed_work_autocancel() so that the work is fully
drained before devres_release_all() detaches dev->devres_head, allowing
any devm resources registered by the delayed work to be released in
proper reverse order. Also only schedule detect_work when
check_populated_dimms() returns -EAGAIN so that probe failure paths do
not leave delayed work pending.
title: hwmon: (peci/dimmtemp) Fix devres leak and UAF on concurrent unbind

desc:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

hwmon: (lm87) Fix drvdata type confusion in vrm_show() and vrm_store()

When an LM87 or ADM1024 device is probed with VID support enabled, reading
from or writing to the vrm sysfs attribute triggers a driver data type
confusion in vrm_show() and vrm_store() in drivers/hwmon/lm87.c.

In lm87_probe(), the driver stores the struct lm87_data pointer on the I2C
client via i2c_set_clientdata() and passes the struct i2c_client pointer as
the drvdata argument to devm_hwmon_device_register_with_groups(), which
attaches the attribute groups to the registered hwmon device with client as
its driver_data. Unlike the other sysfs callbacks that retrieve client via
dev_get_drvdata() and then obtain data via i2c_get_clientdata(), vrm_show()
and vrm_store() assign dev_get_drvdata(dev) directly to struct lm87_data *.
Dereferencing data->vrm therefore accesses the struct i2c_client instance
at offsetof(struct lm87_data, vrm), causing vrm_show() to leak an unrelated
byte from struct i2c_client to userspace and vrm_store() to corrupt a byte
within struct i2c_client while failing to update the actual VRM value.

Fix the problem by assigning the return value from dev_get_drvdata(dev) to
struct i2c_client *client and using i2c_get_clientdata() to get the actual
client data.
title: hwmon: (lm87) Fix drvdata type confusion in vrm_show() and vrm_store()

desc:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

hwmon: chipcap2: fix IRQ teardown ordering

The threaded IRQs are currently requested before the hwmon device
is registered. Since devres releases resources in reverse order,
the hwmon device is unregistered before the IRQs are freed during
driver teardown. An IRQ may therefore still run after the hwmon
device has been released and access the stale data->hwmon pointer.

Separate IRQ discovery from IRQ registration so that the IRQ numbers
and alarm visibility flags are initialized before registering the
hwmon device while the IRQs are released before the hwmon device
during devres cleanup.
title: hwmon: chipcap2: fix IRQ teardown ordering

desc:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

hwmon: (aquacomputer_d5next) reject short status reports

The HID raw_event callback runs before HID core validates the received
report length. aqc_raw_event() reads device-specific status fields at fixed
offsets, including multi-byte values, without first ensuring that the
received buffer contains every field. A truncated report can therefore
cause out-of-bounds reads and update hwmon state with unrelated data.

The required length differs between supported devices and cannot be
derived from the HID report descriptor. Define the minimum length needed
by each asynchronous status format, select it while configuring the
device, and reject reports that do not contain the last field accessed by
that format. Keep the published length zero until probe configuration is
complete, which also excludes legacy devices whose status is retrieved
through feature reports.
title: hwmon: (aquacomputer_d5next) reject short status reports

desc:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

nvme: Do not drop the cdev reference twice when cdev_device_add() fails

Since commit 9952f3882ecb ("nvme: fix cdev lifetime"),
nvme_add_ns_cdev() and nvme_add_ns_head_cdev() take a reference to the
namespace (or namespace head) before calling nvme_cdev_add(), to be
dropped by the char device's release, nvme_cdev_rel(), and drop it
themselves when nvme_cdev_add() fails. But when cdev_device_add()
fails, nvme_cdev_add() has already put the device, and nvme_cdev_rel()
has already dropped that reference: the caller drops it a second time.

With one allocation failure injected into cdev_device_add() for a
namespace on an NVMe over loop controller, deleting the controller
gives, with native multipath:

  BUG: KASAN: slab-use-after-free in nvme_put_ns_head+0x21/0x140
  Write of size 4 at addr ff1100000a4ea078 by task init/1
   nvme_put_ns_head
   nvme_put_ns
   nvme_remove_namespaces
   nvme_do_delete_ctrl
   nvme_delete_ctrl_sync
   nvme_sysfs_delete
  Freed by task 1:
   kfree
   nvme_ns_remove
   nvme_remove_namespaces
  refcount_t: underflow; use-after-free.

Take the reference in nvme_cdev_add() instead, right before
cdev_device_add(), and let the callers neither take nor drop it. Add
nvme_is_ns_cdev() for the check that nvme_cdev_rel() and nvme_cdev_add()
now share.
title: nvme: Do not drop the cdev reference twice when cdev_device_add() fails

desc:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

nvme-rdma: fix NULL queue->ctrl dereference on reconnect

Since commit 2a8513091d2f ("nvme-rdma: parallelize I/O queue allocation
and startup"), a reconnect that gets more I/O queues than before grows
the tag set before the new queues are set up. queue->ctrl is only set
by nvme_rdma_setup_io_queues(), so I/O submitted in between reaches
nvme_rdma_queue_rq() on a queue that was never allocated and
dereferences a NULL queue->ctrl:

  BUG: kernel NULL pointer dereference, address: 000000000000034c
  RIP: 0010:nvme_rdma_queue_rq+0x52/0xb90

Set queue->ctrl for every queue when allocating the controller. Such
requests are then requeued like on any other queue that is not live.
title: nvme-rdma: fix NULL queue->ctrl dereference on reconnect

desc:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

KVM: x86/mmu: Cap number of parent PTEs per SP at 1000 (the arbitrary rmap limit)

When potentially reusing a shadow page, zap the shadow page if its number
of parent PTEs exceeds KVM's (mostly) arbitrary rmap recycling threshold.
Letting the guest create a (mostly) unbounded number of parent PTEs allows
the guest to coerce KVM into creating lists containing millions of PTEs,
effectively bounded only by the maximum number of shadow pages.

Because PTE lists are simple singly linked lists, removal is O(n).  Even
worse, if a list is constructed just so, teardown can be O(n^2), e.g. if
SPTEs are built such that zapping child SPTEs always zaps the last entry
in the list.  To cap things off, all paths that walk PTE lists do so
while holding mmu_lock, without conditionally rescheduling.

Using a doubly linked list would not address the issue, as removal would
remain O(n) since KVM still wouldn't know where in the list to remove from.
Removal could be made O(1) by storing a per-SPTE pointer, but that would
largely defeat the purpose of reusing SPs, and would penalize well-behaved
guests, especially for nested TDP where aliasing page tables is uncommon.

So, cap the maximum number of parent PTEs at the rmap limit.  In practice,
well-behaved guests will likely never run afoul of the limit.  E.g. when
running Linux as L1 with TDP, the number of parent PTEs for a single SP
tops out at under 200 (though undoubtedly obscure workloads can push it
higher).  Deliberately use a "greater than or equal" as opposed to rmap's
strictly "greater than", as the rmap code checks the threshold immediately
*after* inserting into the list, i.e. the limit is 1000 for rmaps, KVM just
very briefly blows past it.

Apply the check to both indirect and direct SPs, because while a fully
direct MMU naturally limits the number of parent PTEs to '1', direct SPs in
indirect MMUs have no such constraint.  E.g. if the guest maps a huge PTE
into many locations in its page tables, and KVM is backing the hugepage
with a direct SP, i.e. with a series of smaller pages, then KVM could end
up with a direct SP with many parents.

Note, shadow_mmu_try_split_huge_pages() always restarts the rmap walk or
bails entirely if it gets to the point where it tries to grab a SP, i.e.
there is *no* pre-existing bug that would be tripped by zapping a SP and
thus rmaps when getting a SP.
title: KVM: x86/mmu: Cap number of parent PTEs per SP at 1000 (the arbitrary rmap limit)

desc:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

KVM: nVMX: Process each host MSR entry at most once when unwinding failed VM-Entry

Add a missing "break" in the inner for-loop of the open coded mess that
unwinds MSRs back to the pre-VM-Enter state when VMLAUNCH/VMRESUME VM-Fails
due to a consistency check that is caught by hardware but missed by KVM.
I.e. move on to the next MSR in the VM-Entry load list after performing a
write using a value found in the VM-Exit load list.  Processing *every*
matching entry in the VM-Exit load list makes the processing quadratic,
which is problematic if the load lists are full of MSRs that are expensive
to emulate.  E.g. writing APIC_BASE triggers kvm_recalculate_apic_map() and
a whole pile of unnecessary work.

Functionally, arbitrarily restoring the value of the first matching entry
is "fine", because none of this is architecturally correct: the load lists
are never supposed to have been used in the first place.  In practice, it's
likely a moot point as no well-behaved VMM will have multiple, diverging
entries in the load lists.
title: KVM: nVMX: Process each host MSR entry at most once when unwinding failed VM-Entry

desc:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

KVM: x86: Conditionally resched when restarting REP string emulation

When restarting emulation, e.g. of a REP-prefixed string instruction,
conditionally reschedule as emulating guest writes can be deceptively slow
and expensive, e.g. when shadow paging is in use and each write can trigger
write tracking.

In a perfect world, restarting emulation (or not) would be less arbitrary,
e.g. would honor not only host events (NEED_RESCHED, signals, etc.) but
also guest events (e.g. by checking kvm_vcpu_has_events()).  Unfortunately,
as pointed out by Sashiko, pio_in_emulated()'s read-ahead logic is baked
into the restart logic, as KVM relies on restarting emulation to drain the
cache and avoid duplicate reads from the I/O port.  I.e. re-entering the
guest on kvm_vcpu_has_events() or __xfer_to_guest_mode_work_pending() would
introduce architecturally-incorrect, guest-visible changes.
title: KVM: x86: Conditionally resched when restarting REP string emulation

desc:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

KVM: x86/mmu: Conditionally resched when retrying gPTE walk on A/D update failure

Conditionally reschedule when retrying a guest PTE walk because the CMPXCHG
to update A/D bits failed, e.g. because a different task/vCPU modified the
relevant gPTEs.  On kernels without involuntary preemption of some kind, a
misbehaving guest can "capture" a pCPU effectively indefinitely and trigger
soft lockups by continuously modifying its gPTEs such that the result of
the walk is remains valid.
title: KVM: x86/mmu: Conditionally resched when retrying gPTE walk on A/D update failure

desc:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

mm: memory: fix truncation removing mapped folios

Ayush reported an issue that shmem/tmpfs folios are still mapped when
truncating them on production:
"
BUG: Bad page cache in process ...  pfn:...
page dumped because: still mapped when deleted
"

I reproduced the issue with Ayush's reproducer [1] with the latest
mm-unstable branch, and I got the following crash info.  From the dump
message, we can see that truncate_inode_folio() is really trying to remove
mapped folios, which is incorrect.

"
[  189.171977] page: refcount:3 mapcount:1 mapping:00000000fe168ee1
index:0x3880 pfn:0x191647
[  189.171995] memcg:ffff0000cc073d40
[  189.171997] aops:shmem_aops ino:3c01 dentry name(?):"memfd:runsc-memory"
[  189.172006] flags: 0x17fffef0002022d(locked|referenced|uptodate|lru|
workingset|swapbacked|node=0|zone=2|lastcpupid=0x3ffff)
.......
[  189.172017] page dumped because: VM_BUG_ON_FOLIO(folio_mapped(folio))
[  189.172026] ------------[ cut here ]------------
[  189.172027] kernel BUG at mm/filemap.c:155!
[  189.172057] Internal error: Oops - BUG: 00000000f2000800 [#1]  SMP
.......
[  189.177721] CPU: 3 UID: 0 PID: 5521 Comm: repro Kdump: loaded Tainted:
7.3.0-rc4+ #277 PREEMPT(lazy)
.......
[  189.183986] Call trace:
[  189.184124]  filemap_unaccount_folio+0xf0/0x1e8 (P)
[  189.184391]  __filemap_remove_folio+0x34/0x160
[  189.184633]  filemap_remove_folio+0x4c/0xb0
[  189.184859]  truncate_inode_folio+0x34/0x58
[  189.185087]  shmem_undo_range+0x220/0x658
[  189.185308]  shmem_fallocate+0x2f0/0x470
[  189.185527]  vfs_fallocate+0x128/0x328
......
[  189.187078]  el0t_64_sync+0x184/0x188
"

After analysis, I believe the race exists between truncation and
MADV_DONTNEED, and shmem's ->map_pages() merely makes the issue easier to
reproduce.  Since MADV_DONTNEED synchronously releases the pagetable page
before calling tlb_flush_rmaps(), this could cause another thread's
truncation to skip zap_pte_range() (due to pmd is none) but still observe
the folio's mapcount as non-zero.  A possible race scenario is as follows:

CPU 0                           CPU 1
shmem_fallocate                 madvise_dontneed_single_vma
  unmap_mapping_range            .......
  ......
  (filemap_map_pages() remap folios)
				  zap_pte_range
  truncate_inode_folio		    zap_empty_pte_table(pmd clear)
    unmap_mapping_folio
    ......
      zap_pmd_range (saw pmd none, skip)

  filemap_remove_folio
    BUG_ON(folio_mapped)
                                    tlb_flush_rmaps(remove rmaps)

To fix this issue, we should move the pmd clear operation (via
zap_empty_pte_table()) to after tlb_flush_rmaps() and use
sync_with_folio_pmd_zap() to sync with concurrent zapping, so that when we
find a pmd_none() while unmapping a folio without holding the PTL, the
folio's mappings are guaranteed to have been removed via
tlb_flush_rmaps().

Meanwhile move the second pmd_none() check to where it belongs: if
splitting zapped the PMD.
title: mm: memory: fix truncation removing mapped folios

desc:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ipv6: reject wrapped temporary address preferred lifetimes

ipv6_create_tempaddr() raises a temporary address's preferred lifetime to
regen_advance + age + 1 when the configured lifetime is too short. The
result is stored in a u32, while regen_advance and age are unsigned long.
If the sum wraps or is truncated, the stored lifetime can still be less
than or equal to regen_advance + age.

addrconf_verify_rtnl() then sees the new address as due for regeneration
and creates another one. Temporary addresses are not limited by
max_addresses since commit 4b08a8f1bd8c ("ipv6: remove max_addresses
check from ipv6_create_tempaddr"), so this can cause unbounded address
growth. With dad_transmits set to -1, a baseline kernel reached 2859
loopback addresses in two seconds.

After storing the adjusted lifetime, verify that it is still greater than
regen_advance + age. Reject the new address if the check fails.

On an x86-64 KASAN kernel, the normal configuration created three IPv6
addresses. The negative dad_transmits, positive multiplication overflow,
and large retransmission-time cases each left only the loopback and public
addresses. An i386 defconfig and an x86-64 allmodconfig both built
addrconf.o with W=1.
title: ipv6: reject wrapped temporary address preferred lifetimes

desc:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

mm/hugetlb: fix mremap deadlock when PMD sharing is possible

move_hugetlb_page_tables() holds the mapping's i_mmap_rwsem for
write while moving hugetlb PTEs. This prevents races with truncation
and protects huge_pmd_unshare(), but the move loop must not call
helpers that can acquire the same rwsem for read.

huge_pte_alloc() can do that when the destination can use PMD
sharing: it may call huge_pmd_share(), which takes i_mmap_rwsem for
read while searching for a shareable PMD table. Calling it while the
move path already holds i_mmap_rwsem for write can deadlock.

Avoid that path for PMD-sized hugetlb mappings that can use PMD
sharing. Instead of allocating or sharing the destination page table
while moving, zap the source range and let the destination fault path
populate or share the PMD lazily.

Reuse the hugetlb unmap logic for the source-side zap by splitting
the core loop out of __unmap_hugepage_range(). The wrapper keeps the
existing tlb_start_vma(), tlb_end_vma() and huge_pmd_unshare_flush()
behavior, while move_hugetlb_page_tables() can reuse the unmap loop
with its existing mmu_gather.
title: mm/hugetlb: fix mremap deadlock when PMD sharing is possible

desc:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

mm/page-writeback: avoid 32-bit overflow in dirty threshold shares

The ratios used by __wb_calc_thresh() are scaled to parts per million, but
the threshold and ratio operands are unsigned long.  On 32-bit kernels,
their multiplication can wrap before the result is assigned to u64.

For example, with a threshold of 25600 pages and the default maximum ratio
of 1000000, wb_max_thresh becomes 4125 pages instead of 25600.  The shared
threshold and minimum share calculations can overflow in the same way,
producing incorrect per-writeback dirty limits.

Use a u64 threshold for the three ratio multiplications and div_u64() to
retain the existing division order and rounding.
title: mm/page-writeback: avoid 32-bit overflow in dirty threshold shares

desc:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

mm: fix address wraparound when scanning large folio PTEs

numa_rebuild_large_mapping() and do_swap_page() can be tricked into
generating an address wraparound, crashing the kernel. All that's required
is to map a tail page of a large folio close enough to the start/end of
the address space to e.g., make

	unsigned long addr_start = addr - (nr << PAGE_SHIFT);

to wrap around.

Let's fix it by providing a better helper, folio_scan_range(), that
takes care of staying within VMA and page table boundaries while
handling possible wraparounds.

There are some nasty details, like not being able to use pmd_addr_end()
in this context. Add some helpful comments for these cases.
title: mm: fix address wraparound when scanning large folio PTEs

desc:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

mm/khugepaged: flush deferred unmaps before dropping a failed folio

collapse_file() can fail its reference-count or dirty-folio check after
unmapping with TTU_BATCH_FLUSH.  Both paths put back the isolated folio,
then unlock it and drop the lookup reference before reaching the common
try_to_unmap_flush().

The page-cache reference does not keep the folio stable once the lock is
released.  Another collapse can replace and free it.  With its PTEs
already gone, that collapse cannot flush the first task's per-task TLB
batch, and retract_page_tables() skips short or unaligned VMAs.  A CPU can
therefore retain a user translation to the freed folio.  This has been
reproduced with unprivileged MADV_COLLAPSE on a memfd.

Flush at out_unlock while the lookup reference and folio lock are still
held.  The common flush continues to cover the accumulated pagelist on
both success and rollback, preserving batching on successful collapses.
title: mm/khugepaged: flush deferred unmaps before dropping a failed folio

desc:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

inet: frags: limit the truesize of a reassembly queue

The truesize of fragments in a reassembly queue is only bounded by
the per netns ipfrag_high_thresh sysctl, which has no upper limit.

inet_frag_reasm_finish() sums the truesize of all fragments in an int.
If this sum reaches 2^32, it wraps, and the final sk_wmem_alloc
adjustment of the socket owning the reassembled skb can cancel its own
reference, leading to a use-after-free of this socket.

This can be triggered from an unprivileged user/network namespace,
raising ipfrag_high_thresh and using padded TUN packets, which keep
a large truesize after being trimmed by ip_rcv_core().

Track the sum of the truesize of fragments in each queue, and refuse
a fragment that would make it bigger than INT_MAX / 2. Callers kill
the queue on this error. This bound is far above the needs of
legitimate traffic.
title: inet: frags: limit the truesize of a reassembly queue

desc:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

mm/cma: accept memory of multi-range CMA areas

Patch series "mm/cma: accept memory of CMA areas reserved with
memblock_reserve()", v1.

Pages of allocated CMA areas are released to the buddy allocator with
__free_pages(), which does not check for unaccepted memory.

This usually works because memblock accepts the memory it allocates.

However, multi-range CMA areas, used by hugetlb_cma, and fixed CMA areas
requested with cma=<size>@<base> are reserved with memblock_reserve() and
their memory is never accepted.

On TDX and SEV-SNP guests the first access to such a page is fatal.

To ease the backporting, each case is addressed by a separate patch:
- patch 1 accepts the memory of multi-range CMA areas
- patch 2 does the same for the fixed CMA areas

The second patch won't apply cleanly to 6.6 and 6.12, but I believe the
stable team LLMs will take care of that :)


This patch (of 2):

On systems with unaccepted memory, memblock allocations accept the
allocated range, but when cma_declare_contiguous_multi() uses open coded
allocation of multiple ranges, it reserves them with memblock_reserve()
and they are never accepted.

These pages are released to the buddy allocator by cma_activate_area()
with __free_pages() that does not check for unaccepted memory, so the
first access to such a page in a TDX or SEV-SNP guest is fatal.

Accept the memory of each range when it is reserved.
title: mm/cma: accept memory of multi-range CMA areas

desc:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

mm/hugetlb_vmemmap: map the shared tail page writable

page_ref_add_unless_zero() reads the refcount and then updates it with a
cmpxchg.  A lockless get, such as a page cache lookup or a PFN scanner,
can read a non-zero refcount from a page that is then freed and reused as
a hugetlb tail page.  If HVO remaps its struct page to the shared tail
page in between, the cmpxchg writes to read-only vmemmap:

    CPU0 (lockless get)               CPU1
    c = atomic_read(&page->_refcount)
                                      page freed
                                      page allocated as a hugetlb tail
                                      HVO remaps the struct page RO
    try_cmpxchg(&page->_refcount, &c, c + 1)
      -> write fault on read-only vmemmap

The refcount is zero by then and the compare fails, but a compare-and-swap
instruction needs write access whether or not it succeeds.  The kernel
oopses when hugetlb pages are allocated at runtime with HVO enabled while
a lockless get races with it.

Commit bd225530a4c7 ("mm/hugetlb_vmemmap: fix race with speculative PFN
walkers") closed the window with RCU on both sides.  The RCU was removed
together with fake heads, on the wrong belief that it was only needed for
them.

Map the shared tail page writable instead of restoring the RCU.  Every
struct page on it is a tail with a zero refcount, so a late cmpxchg
fails and leaves the page unchanged.  RCU would put rcu_read_lock()
back around every get and synchronize_rcu() back into hugetlb
allocation and freeing.

The cost is the protection against stray writes to tail struct pages.  The
shared page is shared by all hugetlb folios of the same order in the zone,
so such a write now corrupts all of them instead of oopsing.

Bootmem folios optimized when the memmap is set up keep their tails
read-only.  Nothing does a lockless get on them before hugetlb takes them
over.
title: mm/hugetlb_vmemmap: map the shared tail page writable

desc:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

mm/ksm: fix userfaultfd protection during merge and unmerge

KSM loses userfaultfd protection when replace_page() builds a new PTE from
vma->vm_page_prot.  Dropping its uffd bit lets a subsequent write go
through ordinary COW instead of userfaultfd write protection handling. 
For RWP, a merged page also becomes readable without faulting.

Keeping the uffd bit and restoring PAGE_NONE fixes merging, but we also
have to handle unmerging.  An existing KSM page can be protected with RWP
before MADV_UNMERGEABLE, so unmerging already needs fixing independently
of preserving RWP during merging.

Unsharing replaces a shared page with a private one and should leave
userfaultfd protection in place, as do_wp_page() already does for write
protection.  Currently, an unshare fault reaches do_uffd_rwp() before it
can proceed to do_wp_page().

- With synchronous RWP, handle_userfault() returns VM_FAULT_SIGBUS.
  break_ksm() then reports success with a KSM page still merged.

- With asynchronous RWP, protection is cleared before unsharing.

Preserve the uffd bit when merging, and restore PAGE_NONE for RWP.  Let
FAULT_FLAG_UNSHARE skip RWP fault handling and keep PAGE_NONE on each
private copy as well.  Unsharing can then complete with RWP still armed
for a subsequent access.
title: mm/ksm: fix userfaultfd protection during merge and unmerge

desc:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

mm/vma: write lock source VMA before duplicating it in __split_vma()

__split_vma() duplicates the source VMA before taking its VMA write lock,
and until the VMA is write-locked, a concurrent thread might set
VMA_MAYBE_GUARD_BIT, resulting in the duplication missing the flag.

If this happens, then fork may fail to duplicate guard markers and, if a
file-backed mapping, THP collapse may also discard the markers.

Resolve this by taking the VMA write lock before vm_area_dup() and, since
all callers of vm_area_dup() now hold the VMA write lock, assert that this
is the case there, and add a comment to explain why it's needed.

[ljs@kernel.org: add VMA write assert in vm_area_dup(), commit message touchup]
title: mm/vma: write lock source VMA before duplicating it in __split_vma()

desc:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ocfs2: find the xattr entry again after defragmenting a bucket

ocfs2_xattr_set_entry_bucket() hands loc.xl_entry to ocfs2_xa_set() twice:
once for the bucket as it stands, and, if that reports -ENOSPC, once more
after ocfs2_defrag_xattr_bucket() has packed the name/value pairs down.

Defragmenting ends by sorting the entry array on xe_name_hash.  Buckets
are kept sorted, so the sort only permutes entries that share a hash, but
lib/sort.c is an unstable heapsort and it does permute them.  loc.xl_entry
is an address inside xh_entries[], so afterwards it denotes whichever
entry landed in that slot rather than the one the search found.

The second ocfs2_xa_set() then works on the wrong entry.  Nothing on that
path compares the entry's name with xi->xi_name, so what happens depends
on how the two entries compare in size: ocfs2_xa_reuse_entry() trips its
BUG_ON() when the padded name sizes differ, and otherwise the new value is
written into the neighbouring attribute's value slot while the attribute
being set is left untouched.  setxattr() reports success either way.

Remember the entry's hash before defragmenting and look the entry up
again afterwards, the way ocfs2_xattr_bucket_find() does.  An entry that
cannot be found again means the bucket no longer holds what the search
found, so fail with -EFSCORRUPTED rather than writing through the stale
pointer.
title: ocfs2: find the xattr entry again after defragmenting a bucket

desc:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

mm: memcontrol: fix NULL pointer deref and UAF from high_work_func() on dying memcg

When memory.high is exceeded in non-task context, try_charge_memcg()
schedules memcg->high_work without taking a reference on the memcg, and
high_work_func() invokes reclaim_high() without pinning the memcg.

With obj_cgroup reparenting, introduced in commit bf4f059954dc ("mm:
memcg/slab: obj_cgroup API"), objects charged to a child memcg are
reparented to its parent in mem_cgroup_css_offline() instead of holding a
reference on the child until uncharged.  Subsequent uncharges of those
objects go to the parent, which can leave the child's memory use
permanently above its high limit, so any later charge on the offlined
memcg in non-task context schedules high_work.  This was later widened
from kernel memory to LRU folios when commit f1cf8d2f36dc ("mm:
memcontrol: eliminate the problem of dying memory cgroup for LRU folios")
converted LRU folios to use obj_cgroup reparenting.

cancel_work_sync(&memcg->high_work) only runs at the end of teardown in
mem_cgroup_css_free(), so high_work_func() can start or still be running
reclaim_high() after mem_cgroup_css_released() or shrink_many() has called
lru_gen_release_memcg() and unhashed lruvec->lrugen.list.  If reclaim
tries to rotate the memcg, lru_gen_rotate_memcg() dereferences a NULL
pprev pointer.  This issue is specific to MGLRU and was introduced with
the memcg LRU in commit e4dde56cd208 ("mm: multi-gen LRU: per-node
lru_gen_folio lists").

With either traditional LRU or MGLRU, css_free_rwork_fn() calls
css_rstat_exit() which frees per-CPU rstat data before calling
mem_cgroup_css_free().  If reclaim_high() is still running, rstat updates
via mod_lruvec_state() -> __css_rstat_updated() cause a use-after-free on
the per-CPU rstat data.  This was introduced when commit 5da3bfa029d6
("cgroup: use separate rstat trees for each subsystem") moved
css_rstat_exit() ahead of ss->css_free().

Fix both problems by acquiring a reference with css_tryget_online() in
high_work_func() before calling reclaim_high(), and by resetting
memory.high and swap.high to PAGE_COUNTER_MAX in mem_cgroup_css_offline()
so that charges via references on an offlined memcg do not trigger
high_work on the dead child and skip checking live ancestors in
try_charge_memcg().

Acquiring the reference in high_work_func() rather than before scheduling
high_work is safe because mem_cgroup_css_free() calls irq_work_sync() and
cancel_work_sync() which cancels pending work and waits for an already
running high_work_func() to complete before mem_cgroup_free() frees the
memcg.  css_tryget_online() uses percpu_ref_tryget_live() and is safe to
call after percpu_ref_exit() before the cgroup is freed unlike
css_tryget().

desc:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

mm/cma: accept memory of CMA areas reserved at a fixed address

CMA areas allocated from memblock have their memory accepted by
memblock_alloc_range_nid(), but areas reserved at a fixed address with
memblock_reserve() are not.

If a fixed CMA area is requested by the cma=<size>@<base> command line
parameter, it may be in regular RAM and on TDX and SEV-SNP guests it
must be accepted.

Accept the memory of fixed CMA areas as well, so that all CMA areas are
accepted regardless of how they were reserved.
title: mm/cma: accept memory of CMA areas reserved at a fixed address

desc:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ocfs2: cache the mount context for dentry lock callbacks

ocfs2_drop_dentry_lock() drops the inode reference before releasing the
DENTRY lock.  This lets inode eviction release the local inode and open
locks before a remote unlink can proceed past the DENTRY lock.

A DLM callback can still arrive before the DENTRY lock has been dropped.
ocfs2_get_dentry_osb() obtains the mount context through dl_inode->i_sb,
which can access a freed inode when the downconvert thread drops the
last inode reference in its post-unlock callback:

  Downconvert thread                     DLM callback thread
  ------------------                     -------------------
  ocfs2_process_blocked_lock()
    ocfs2_dentry_post_unlock()
      ocfs2_dentry_lock_put()
        ocfs2_drop_dentry_lock()
          iput(dl->dl_inode)
          [inode reclaimed after RCU]
                                         ocfs2_blocking_ast()
                                           ocfs2_get_dentry_osb()
                                             dl->dl_inode->i_sb
          ocfs2_simple_drop_lockres()

Store the mount context in the DENTRY lock resource's l_priv field and use
the default mount-context lookup.  Recover the containing dentry lock with
container_of(), as already done for refcount locks, and remove
ocfs2_get_dentry_osb().  ocfs2_dismount_volume() shuts down the DLM before
freeing the mount context, so callbacks can use it without accessing the
inode.  Preserve the existing iput-before-unlock order to avoid delaying
local inode and open lock release until after the DENTRY lock is released.
title: ocfs2: cache the mount context for dentry lock callbacks

desc:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ocfs2/cluster: unlink socket containers before releasing resources

A socket container's node and socket must remain alive while the
container is on sock_containers. The debugfs formatter reads sc_node
and sc_sock under o2net_debug_lock without taking their references, but
sc_kref_release() releases both before taking that lock to unlink the
container.

With CONFIG_DEBUG_FS enabled, a synchronous sender can retain its last
socket-container reference after o2net_disconnect_node() has detached
the connection and flushed o2net_wq. The caller runs outside that
workqueue. After the sender removes its configfs dependency, node
removal can proceed without waiting for the sender's final sc_put():

  Sender (final sc_put)    Configfs rmdir        Debugfs reader
  --------------------    --------------        --------------
  o2nm_undepend_item()
                          Drop node item refs
  o2nm_node_put()
    [node can be freed]
                                               sc_seq_show()
                                                 Lock debug lock
                                                 Read sc_node->nd_name
                                                 Unlock debug lock
  sc_node = NULL
  o2net_debug_del_sc()

The earlier socket release has a similar window. The container is
still selectable while its socket has been released and sc_sock has
not yet been cleared:

  Sender (final sc_put)                       Debugfs reader
  --------------------                       --------------
  sock_release(sc->sc_sock)
    [socket can be freed]
                                             sc_seq_show()
                                               Lock debug lock
                                               Read sc_sock->sk fields
                                               Unlock debug lock
  sc_sock = NULL
  ...
  o2net_debug_del_sc()

Move o2net_debug_del_sc() before releasing either resource. Unlinking
under the existing debug lock waits for an active formatter to finish
and prevents later readers from selecting the container. This covers
both socket fields and node fields, including nd_num in the stats
formatter.

desc:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ocfs2: stop recovery before shutting down local allocators

Recovery completion needs the local allocators until it has finished
reclaiming a failed node's allocation window and truncate log.  During
unmount, quota recovery is stopped first, but that leaves recovery_state
at OCFS2_REC_QUOTA_DISABLED.  New non-quota recovery can still start.

ocfs2_truncate_log_shutdown() drains existing completion work and releases
osb_tl_bh before ocfs2_recovery_exit() closes that publication path:

  Unmount                             Recovery
  -------                             --------
  stop quota recovery; disable quotas
  truncate_log_shutdown()
    flush existing completion work
                                      recover another failed node
                                        queue completion
    flush local log; release buffer
                                      complete_truncate_log_recovery()
                                        use released osb_tl_bh
  recovery_exit(): disable and drain

An extra buffer reference alone would still let completion append new
records after the final truncate-log flush.

Split stopping and draining recovery from freeing its state. Stop all
recovery producers and drain completion work before shutting down either
local allocator. Keep recovery-state release at its existing later point,
so its lifetime relative to other teardown users stays unchanged. The
second stop at recovery_exit() is harmless once recovery is disabled.

desc:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ocfs2/dlm: serialize migration MLE cleanup on failure

A migration MLE has a base reference for the mastering answer and an
in-use reference held by dlm_migrate_lockres(). The finishing assertion
consumes the base reference, but migration failure drops it again
without checking whether the assertion already consumed it.

The target queues its migration worker before it acknowledges the
ALL_DONE packet, so its finishing assertion can be handled while the
sender still waits for the status. If the connection fails before the
status arrives, dlm_send_one_lockres() returns an error for a migration
that the target has already completed:

  Old-master sender                  Finishing assertion
  -----------------                  -------------------
  publish MLE; take in-use reference
  send ALL_DONE; wait for status
                                     take lookup reference
                                     unlink MLE
                                     put lookup and base references
  send returns a connection error
  put base reference again; free MLE
  put in-use reference; access freed MLE

dlm_assert_master_handler() holds dlm->spinlock from the MLE lookup to
the final puts, and it takes dlm->master_lock around the unlink and the
puts. Decide under the same locks: if the MLE is already unhashed, the
assertion consumed the base reference, so drop only the sender's in-use
reference. Otherwise unlink it before consuming the base reference so a
later assertion no longer finds it.

An assertion that got there first has also made the target the owner
and cleared DLM_LOCK_RES_MIGRATING. Treating the attempt as failed at
that point would leave the lockres owned by the target while this node
still holds the other nodes' locks and refmap bits, so it could neither
be purged nor migrated again. Finish our side as a completed migration
does instead: drop those locks under res->spinlock if the target still
owns the lockres, and recalculate its usage.

Use the same cleanup for the pre-send failure, the send failure and the
target-death failure paths. The sender's in-use reference keeps the MLE
alive until its final put outside the nested locks. Successful
migration retains its existing in-use-only put.

A target that has died cannot assert after the sender has seen its
death. The o2net node-down callback runs before the DLM one; it
disconnects the node and flushes the workqueue that runs the message
handlers, so an assertion already received has been handled by the time
the DLM removes the node from the domain map. A node that leaves the
domain cleanly sends its exit message only after its assertions have
been answered.

Two windows of the hand-over itself are left as they are: the handler
switches the owner and the sender drops the other nodes' locks moments
later, and an assertion from a live target that arrives after the
sender has given up still meets the owner check in the handler. Waiting
for the target before giving up would only stretch the first window
into the time in which recovery of the target can observe it.

KASAN report, only the relevant frames are kept:

Read of size 8 at addr ffff8881190e3c20 by task umount/593

desc:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ocfs2: do not index before the entry array when dividing an empty bucket

ocfs2_divide_xattr_bucket() appends an empty bucket carrying a sentinel
hash when the source bucket has no divide position, taking that hash
from xh_entries[start - 1].  ocfs2_xattr_find_divide_pos() returns count
when every entry shares one hash, and its loop does not run at all for
count < 2, so an empty bucket comes back with start == count == 0 and
the read is xh_entries[-1].

That is outside the __counted_by_le(xh_count) bounds of xh_entries[] and
lands on the header, so the value picked up is
xh_count | xh_free_start << 16.  One above it is written into the new
bucket's xh_entries[0] and committed, which leaves a bucket whose first
hash does not follow the bucket before it.  ocfs2_xattr_bucket_find()
binary searches on xh_entries[0], so the broken key hides the range the
sentinel was meant to cover: getxattr() answers -ENODATA for an
attribute that is stored, and an insert can go to the wrong bucket and
leave two copies of a name.  The cross cluster divide hands the same
value back as a tree record's e_cpos, which then claims a hash range it
does not cover.

Read xh_entries[0] instead.  The branch is only reached when every entry
shares one hash, so for a non-empty bucket it holds the same value, and
for an empty one it is the slot that carries the bucket key.

An empty bucket reaches the divide from
ocfs2_check_xattr_bucket_collision(), which reports no collision for
one, through ocfs2_add_new_xattr_bucket() and
ocfs2_extend_xattr_bucket().  It does not take a failed set to get
there: a divide that finds no position is itself what leaves an empty
sentinel bucket behind, and a later extend can pick it as the target.
title: ocfs2: do not index before the entry array when dividing an empty bucket

desc:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ocfs2: find the xattr entry again after converting a block to a bucket

ocfs2_xattr_create_index_block() turns a non-indexed xattr block into a
tree by copying it into a bucket, and the copy sorts the entries: a
block holds them in insertion order, a bucket by name hash.
ocfs2_xattr_update_xattr_search() nevertheless relocates the caller's
search by the index the entry had in the block, so unless the two orders
agreed it points at an unrelated entry, and nothing between there and
the write compares that entry's name with the one being set.

Setting an xattr whose new value no longer fits the block arrives here
with xs->not_found clear.  The block gave up because
ocfs2_xa_block_can_reuse() wants an exact namevalue size match, while
ocfs2_xa_bucket_can_reuse() only wants an entry at least as large as the
new one, so the bucket accepts a pair the block rejected and the update
lands on whichever entry the sort left at that index.  Equal padded name
lengths get that other attribute's value replaced in place and its name
left alone, so setxattr returns success while the attribute asked for
keeps its old value.  A longer one trips ocfs2_xa_reuse_entry()'s
BUG_ON, and a shorter one is refused by the bucket as well, so
ocfs2_xa_prepare_entry() wipes the entry and writes the new name over
it, leaving xe_name_hash describing a name that is no longer there.

Find the entry again by the name being set, matching the type as well.
The copy carries every entry and every name over unchanged, and (type,
name) pairs are unique within a block, so the match is exact.  The type
matters because the handlers strip their prefix before calling
ocfs2_xattr_set(), so user.foo and trusted.foo share a stored name, a
stored length and a hash, and both can sit in the same block.

The name has to come from xi rather than from xs->here: a failed set can
remove the entry xs->here names, and only the "growing" caller sets
ctxt->set_abort, which is what stops the conversion.  Scan every entry
rather than narrowing on the hash the way ocfs2_find_xe_in_bucket()
does, since an existing entry keeps the hash it was stored under, which
a kernel that sign-extended the name bytes made different from the one
computed now.  An empty result means the entry did not survive the
failed set and this has become an insert; leaving xs->here alone would
keep it pointing into the block, which is rewritten as a tree root
before the caller reads it again.
title: ocfs2: find the xattr entry again after converting a block to a bucket

desc:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

vhost: fix used ring index wrap in vhost_add_used_n_in_order

vhost_add_used_n_in_order() advances start by nheads[i] but wraps it
with a single subtraction.  If start + nheads[i] >= 2 * vq->num, start
can remain outside the ring.

With used-ring logging enabled, start > vq->num makes (vq->num - start)
underflow.  log_write() then sets bits beyond the dirty-log bitmap,
potentially corrupting adjacent userspace memory.  This is reachable on
the vhost-net TX path with VIRTIO_F_IN_ORDER: done_idx can reach
VHOST_NET_BATCH (64), triggering the issue with a 32-entry ring.

Wrap start with a mask to keep it within the ring.  VHOST_SET_VRING_NUM
enforces a nonzero power-of-two ring size, allowing start to be wrapped
using & (vq->num - 1).
title: vhost: fix used ring index wrap in vhost_add_used_n_in_order

desc:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

virtio_blk: use synchronous quiesce in virtblk_freeze_priv()

blk_mq_run_work_fn() can call blk_mq_sched_dispatch_requests() through
blk_mq_run_dispatch_ops(). The dispatcher checks QUEUE_FLAG_QUIESCED
while the flag is clear. It can then be preempted before it gets a
request. At that time, it has no queue usage reference, so
blk_mq_freeze_queue() does not wait for it.

virtblk_freeze_priv() then calls blk_mq_quiesce_queue_nowait() and
blk_mq_unfreeze_queue(). A new request can enter the queue. The old
dispatcher can run again, use its old flag check, get the new request,
and call virtio_queue_rq(). At the same time, virtblk_freeze_priv() can
reset the device, delete the virtqueues, and free vblk->vqs. The old
dispatcher can then use a deleted virtqueue or a NULL vblk->vqs, and the
kernel can crash.

Fix this by using blk_mq_quiesce_queue(), which waits for dispatch code
that was already running. Keep the existing freeze and unfreeze order.
The queue remains quiesced until virtblk_restore_priv() calls
blk_mq_unquiesce_queue().
title: virtio_blk: use synchronous quiesce in virtblk_freeze_priv()

desc:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

vduse: fix VA/PA confusion in the coherent page fault path

vduse_domain_get_coherent_page() assumes that iotlb entries above
bounce_size were installed by vduse_domain_alloc_coherent(), so it
treats map->addr as a physical address. But vduse registers with
use_va = true, and when the device is bound to vhost_vdpa,
vhost_vdpa_va_map() stores a userspace virtual address in map->addr,
which vduse_domain_set_map() then copies into the same iotlb. A
process holding the domain file descriptor across a rebind can
therefore fault in an arbitrary physical page with read/write
access, ignoring the entry permissions.

Additionally, since the domain file mmap lacks VM_IO, the domain
file itself can be mapped and passed to vhost_vdpa_va_map(),
producing self-referential entries that bypass the coherent path
check.

To fix, only translate entries whose backing file is the domain
file itself in vduse_domain_get_coherent_page(), reject such
entries in vduse_domain_set_map() since only external mappings
should be imported, and set VM_IO on the domain file mmap so
vhost_vdpa_va_map() refuses to map it in the first place.
title: vduse: fix VA/PA confusion in the coherent page fault path

desc:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

hwrng: virtio - prevent use-after-free after a failed restore

remove_common() frees the driver data during freeze, but does not clear
vdev->priv, which points to freed memory. If probe_common() then fails
during restore, a later remove or freeze can dereference the dangling
pointer.

Clear vdev->priv on the probe_common() error cleanup path and before
freeing the driver data in remove_common(). Also reset the device and
return early from remove_common() if vdev->priv is already NULL for a
safe teardown after a failed restore.
title: hwrng: virtio - prevent use-after-free after a failed restore

desc:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

iommu/virtio: Reset device before deleting virtqueues on probe failure

viommu_probe() marks the device DRIVER_OK before populating the event
virtqueue and registering the IOMMU device in sysfs.  viommu_fill_evtq()
hands the device a set of device-writable buffers through
virtqueue_add_inbuf(), so from that point on the device may write into
them and into the rings.

If either step fails, the error path deletes the virtqueues without
resetting the device first.  The event buffers are allocated with
devm_kmalloc_array() and are released as probe unwinds, so the device can
go on writing to memory that has been freed.

Reset the device before deleting the virtqueues, the way viommu_remove()
already does.
title: iommu/virtio: Reset device before deleting virtqueues on probe failure

desc:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

vhost-scsi: zero misaligned I/O bounce pages

The misaligned I/O fallback copies the full bounce scatterlist to the
request buffer during completion.  If a data-in command transfers less
than requested, part of a newly allocated bounce page can remain unwritten.

Allocate bounce pages with __GFP_ZERO so all bytes copied during completion
have a defined value.  This path is already the slow fallback for
misaligned I/O, so the added initialization cost is acceptable.

Found during an LLM-assisted source audit and validated with a QEMU/KVM
vhost-scsi target using misaligned data-in commands.
title: vhost-scsi: zero misaligned I/O bounce pages

desc:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

net/sched: sch_qfq: prevent aggregate self-replacement

qfq_change_class() snapshots the current aggregate settings while
holding the qdisc tree lock, but drops the lock before selecting the
destination aggregate. During that gap, qfq_enqueue() can move the
class to an aggregate matching the requested settings.

When qfq_change_class() resumes, qfq_find_agg() then returns cl->agg.
If it is a singleton, qfq_deact_rm_from_agg() frees the aggregate
before qfq_add_to_agg() immediately accesses the same pointer, causing
a use-after-free.

While holding the tree lock, skip the replacement when the destination
is already the current aggregate. Any estimator replacement has already
completed, so the class change can finish normally.
title: net/sched: sch_qfq: prevent aggregate self-replacement

desc:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

xfs: fix temporary cursor leak in btree shift corruption paths

In xfs_btree_lshift and xfs_btree_rshift, when XFS_IS_CORRUPT detects
an invalid firstrec/lastrec result after xfs_btree_dup_cursor has
successfully allocated a temporary cursor, the error path jumps to
error0 which returns without freeing tcur.  This leaks the cursor
memory, the xfs_group reference, and the per-level buffer references
held by the duplicated cursor.  Jump to error1 instead, which calls
xfs_btree_del_cursor(tcur, XFS_BTREE_ERROR) to properly release all
resources.
title: xfs: fix temporary cursor leak in btree shift corruption paths

desc:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

blk-mq: fix out-of-bounds read in blk_mq_free_rqs

A KASAN slab-out-of-bounds read can occur in blk_mq_free_rqs() when there
is a mismatch between the number of hardware queues allocated for the IO
scheduler (et->nr_hw_queues) and the number of hardware queues in the block
tag set (set->nr_hw_queues).

This mismatch can happen if blk_mq_update_nr_hw_queues() fails halfway
through (e.g., due to memory pressure during
blk_mq_prealloc_tag_set_tags()). In this error path, the elevator is
restored with a larger number of hardware queues than the block tag set
actually has.

When the elevator is later freed, blk_mq_free_sched_tags() iterates up to
the new et->nr_hw_queues and calls blk_mq_free_rqs(). In blk_mq_free_rqs(),
it attempts to access set->tags[hctx_idx] to get the driver tags. Because
set->nr_hw_queues was not updated due to the earlier failure, set->tags
still has the old (smaller) size, leading to an out-of-bounds read.

BUG: KASAN: slab-out-of-bounds in blk_mq_free_rqs+0xde/0x680
Read of size 8 at addr ffff88818d67fc28 by task syz-executor117/5839
Call Trace:
 blk_mq_free_rqs+0xde/0x680
 blk_mq_free_map_and_rqs+0x40/0xf0
 blk_mq_free_sched_tags
 blk_mq_free_sched_res+0xeb/0x280
 elevator_change_done+0x1d2/0x5c0
 elevator_change+0x34f/0x480
 elv_iosched_store+0x504/0x630
 queue_attr_store+0x207/0x2b0

To fix this, explicitly check if hctx_idx < set->nr_hw_queues before
accessing set->tags[hctx_idx]. If hctx_idx >= set->nr_hw_queues, the
hardware queue doesn't exist in the tag set, meaning there are no driver
tags to clear mappings from. In this case, safely set drv_tags to NULL. The
subsequent call to blk_mq_clear_rq_mapping() already handles a NULL
drv_tags pointer and will safely return.
title: blk-mq: fix out-of-bounds read in blk_mq_free_rqs

desc:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

net: restore refcount ordering for lockless socket access

Before commit fb041bb7c0a9 ("locking/refcount: Consolidate implementations
of refcount_t"), default builds implemented refcount_inc_not_zero() using
atomic_add_unless(), which provided full memory ordering on success. The
commit removed that ordering on weakly ordered architectures, allowing
accesses after a successful reference acquisition to be reordered before
it.

Use refcount_inc_not_zero_acquire() in the IPv4 and IPv6 established
lookups and in inet_twsk_purge(), where the socket is validated again
after taking a reference.

bpf_sk_assign() can receive a socket pointer obtained through BTF
without a reference. Use acquire ordering when it takes its own reference
for a refcounted socket.

Use refcount_set_release() when setting refcounts in the SYN cookie,
TCP Fast Open, request migration, and TIME_WAIT paths. Keep the existing
TIME_WAIT smp_wmb(), which separately orders the refcount store before
ehash publication.
title: net: restore refcount ordering for lockless socket access

desc:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

can: dev: can_dropped_invalid_skb: drop CAN XL frames on non-CAN XL devices

Sending a PF_PACKET bypasses the CAN framework logic and can directly
reach a CAN driver's xmit() function. The PF_PACKET framework only
checks that skb->len does not exceed the net_device MTU.

For a CAN device that is not CAN XL capable, anything above CANFD_MTU
(72 bytes) is therefore dropped before it reaches the driver. However,
CAN XL frames are variable length. can_is_canxl_skb() accepts lengths in
the range CANXL_HDR_SIZE + CANXL_MIN_DLEN up to CANXL_MTU, i.e. 13 to
2060 bytes.

As a result, an ETH_P_CANXL skb with a length between 13 and 72 bytes
can pass both the MTU and the can_dropped_invalid_skb() checks.

A driver that does not support CAN XL will interpret canxl_frame->flags
as a length because of the overlap with can_frame->len. And because
CANXL_XLF is set, the resulting length is between 128 and 255. For
drivers that do not check can_frame->len before copying can_frame->data,
as most drivers do, this results in a buffer overflow of up to 247
bytes.

Drop ETH_P_CANXL skbs if the device does not have the CAN_CAP_XL
capability. Keep can_is_canxl_skb() for the validation of CAN XL skbs.
title: can: dev: can_dropped_invalid_skb: drop CAN XL frames on non-CAN XL devices

desc:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

nvmet: reject keep-alive timeouts that would overflow

nvmet_set_feat_kato() and nvmet_alloc_ctrl() convert the 32-bit
millisecond KATO from the host to seconds with DIV_ROUND_UP(kato, 1000).
The addition in DIV_ROUND_UP() is done in 32 bits, so any KATO above
4294966296 ms wraps around and rounds to 0 seconds. A Set Features
command with KATO 0xffffffff then succeeds but disables the keep-alive
timer: Get Features returns 0 and Keep Alive fails with Keep Alive
Timeout Invalid. A Connect command with such a KATO creates a controller
without a keep-alive timer.

The converted value has more consumers that can overflow. Get Features
multiplies it by 1000, and the timer paths multiply it by HZ in 32 bits
and arm a delay that must not exceed MAX_JIFFY_OFFSET.

Reject a KATO whose rounded value does not fit all of these. Return Keep
Alive Timeout Invalid from both Set Features and Connect. Validate Set
Features before stopping the current timer so a failed update leaves its
timeout unchanged. Round in 64 bits. A KATO of 0 keeps its current
meaning.
title: nvmet: reject keep-alive timeouts that would overflow

desc:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

xfs: clamp the pNFS layout range to the maximum file size

xfs_fs_map_blocks() lets two bad layout ranges through. An offset of
2^63 or more is negative and passes "offset > limit". A length above
the limit, such as NFS4_UINT64_MAX, wraps "offset > limit - length"
and stays unclamped. With NFS4_UINT64_MAX, a read layout is built from
an uninitialized mapping.

Reject a negative offset and one at the limit, and clamp the length.
This needs "xfs: cap the block count of xfs_iomap_write_direct() at one
extent".
title: xfs: clamp the pNFS layout range to the maximum file size

desc:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

xfs: cap the block count of xfs_iomap_write_direct() at one extent

xfs_iomap_write_direct() reserves blocks for the whole count in an
unsigned int. For a pNFS layout the client chooses that count, and an
RW LAYOUTGET for 16 TiB wraps the reservation and shuts XFS down.

xfs_bmapi_write() maps at most XFS_MAX_BMBT_EXTLEN blocks here, so cap
the count at that. nfsd asks again for the rest. The other callers get
the same mapping as before.
title: xfs: cap the block count of xfs_iomap_write_direct() at one extent

desc:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

xfs: refuse a pNFS LAYOUTCOMMIT of a range without blocks

A client can commit a hole in a LAYOUTCOMMIT, because nfsd does not
check the extents against its layouts. xfs_iomap_write_unwritten() then
allocates written blocks there. A large hole overruns the block
reservation and shuts XFS down. A small one exposes stale data.

Refuse such a range with -EIO, using XFS_BMAPI_CONVERT_ONLY.
title: xfs: refuse a pNFS LAYOUTCOMMIT of a range without blocks

desc:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

xfs: mark the inode preallocated for pNFS write layouts past EOF

xfs_fs_map_blocks() marks the inode XFS_DIFLAG_PREALLOC only when it
allocates blocks for a write layout. A write layout past EOF can also
hand out allocated blocks, such as speculative preallocation. blockgc
then frees them under the layout, and another file may get them.

Mark the inode whenever a write mapping ends past EOF.
title: xfs: mark the inode preallocated for pNFS write layouts past EOF

desc:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

mm/khugepaged: always recheck the pmd in try_collapse_pte_mapped_thp()

try_collapse_pte_mapped_thp() drops the PTE lock after it has cleared the
page table, and takes the PMD lock and the PTE lock to remove it.

In between, MADV_DONTNEED with CONFIG_PT_RECLAIM can reclaim the
page table. The pmd_same() check is supposed to handle this, but it is
only done with CONFIG_SPLIT_PTE_PTLOCKS.

Fix it by performing the check unconditionally.

Fix generated by an LLM and sent by Josef Bacik in private.

[ david: adjust description ]
title: mm/khugepaged: always recheck the pmd in try_collapse_pte_mapped_thp()

desc:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

mm/huge_memory: fix zapping migration entries for device-private THPs

A PMD migration entry can refer to a device-private folio.
zap_huge_pmd_folio() checks the folio type instead of the entry type,
so it treats such a migration entry as a device-private entry.

Installing the migration entry already removed the reverse mapping and
dropped the mapping reference. Zapping it must not repeat those
operations. Concurrent MADV_DONTNEED during migration back to system
memory can trigger this.

Check the PMD entry type using pmd_is_device_private_entry().

Fix generated by an LLM and sent by Chris Mason in private.

[ david: simplify description ]
title: mm/huge_memory: fix zapping migration entries for device-private THPs

desc:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

mm/huge_memory: fix truncate racing with PMD zapping

zap_huge_pmd_folio() removes the rmap before calling folio_mark_dirty().
If this was the last mapping, truncation can skip unmapping the folio
and proceed without waiting for the PMD lock, racing with dirtying.

ifs_set_range_dirty() can oops if MADV_DONTNEED races with
ftruncate() on XFS, when we get the folio set dirty after it was found
to not be mapped anymore.

Move folio_mark_dirty() and folio_mark_accessed() before rmap removal,
matching the PTE zap path. This keeps the folio mapped while updating
its state, so truncation must wait for the page table lock.

Fix generated by an LLM and sent by Chris Mason in private.

[ david: simplify comment and description ]
title: mm/huge_memory: fix truncate racing with PMD zapping

desc:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

can: dev: can_fill_info(): don't wake up controller if interface is down

If the interface is down, the CAN controller might be powered down and
its clocks gated. Don't call do_get_berr_counter() to read the bus error
counters if the interface is down, and adjust can_get_size() to match.

This removes one trigger for a synchronous external abort seen on
i.MX8QXP when "ip link show" is run on a flexcan interface that was
never brought up. The underlying cause is platform-specific: on i.MX8QXP
the CAN clocks are gated through the SCU LPCG and the subsystem shares
the IMX_SC_R_CAN_0 power domain, and there is a window after
pm_runtime_resume_and_get() returns where the clock has not reached the
module yet. This patch avoids the netlink query path while the interface
is down, but does not root-cause the LPCG window itself.

As a result, IFLA_CAN_BERR_COUNTER is no longer reported for down
interfaces. Userspace must treat the attribute as optional.

The issue was triggered on an i.MX8QXP board by running "ip link show"
without ever bringing the interface up:

    Internal error: synchronous external abort: 0000000096000210

    pc : flexcan_read_le+0x0/0x18
    lr : flexcan_get_berr_counter+0x4c/0x8c
    Call trace:
     flexcan_read_le+0x0/0x18
     flexcan_get_berr_counter+0x4c/0x8c
     can_fill_info+0x1f8/0x434
     rtnl_fill_ifinfo+0x8fc/0xbb4
     rtnl_dump_ifinfo+0x364/0x448

This is the same class of problem fixed for m_can in
commit 91a55c72a821 ("can: m_can: m_can_get_berr_counter(): don't
wake up controller if interface is down").
title: can: dev: can_fill_info(): don't wake up controller if interface is down

desc:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

can: raw, isotp: copy socket options outside of lock_sock()

The CAN_RAW and CAN_ISOTP specific socket options are copied from and
to user space while holding lock_sock(). A copy that faults or stalls,
e.g. on a userfaultfd or FUSE backed mapping, holds lock_sock() for its
whole duration.

raw_notify() and isotp_notify() take lock_sock() of a socket that is
bound to the vanishing device while holding RTNL. As the CAN_RAW
options can also be changed on a bound socket, a stalled copy can block
RTNL on an unregistration or namespace change of the bound device.
Before "can: protect the receive lists with a per-device lock",
raw_setsockopt() even held RTNL itself during the copy. CAN_ISOTP only
copies its options for unbound sockets, which isotp_notify() skips
without taking lock_sock().

Keep the user space copies out of the locked sections: Check the option
name and length and copy the option values, including the CAN_RAW_FILTER
filters, to kernel memory before lock_sock(). raw_setsockopt_locked()
and isotp_setsockopt_locked() get the copied values directly and drop
their now redundant length checks and copies. As a side effect, a
failing copy can not leave partially overwritten options behind
anymore. In raw_getsockopt() duplicate the filters under lock_sock() and
copy them to user space after release_sock().

As the option name and length are now checked before lock_sock(), the
order of the checks in isotp_setsockopt() and accordingly the order of
the returned error values changes. This is in line with POSIX, which
does not define an order in which multiple error conditions are
detected and reported.

The generic SOL_SOCKET options in sk_setsockopt() are not affected by
this patch.
title: can: raw, isotp: copy socket options outside of lock_sock()

desc:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

can: protect the receive lists with a per-device lock

The receive lists of a CAN device are located in the device's
can_ml_priv and travel with the device when it is moved to another
network namespace. But they are protected by the per-netns
rcvlists_lock. So can_rx_unregister() needs dev_net(dev) to pick the
right lock and silently returns when the passed namespace does not
match dev_net(dev) anymore.

isotp_release() and bcm_release() leave their notifier list before they
take any lock that serializes against the netdev notifier, which runs
under RTNL. When the bound device is moved to another namespace in this
window, the notifier skips the socket and the release path has to remove
the filters itself. isotp_release() passes the socket's namespace, which
does not match dev_net(dev) anymore. bcm_rx_unreg() passes dev_net(dev),
which can_rx_unregister() reads again for its check, so a namespace
change between both reads makes the check fail as well. In both cases
can_rx_unregister() silently returns. As can_rx_register() stores
rcv->sk without a reference, the remaining receivers point to the freed
socket (isotp) or the freed op (bcm):

  BUG: KASAN: use-after-free in isotp_rcv+0x1570/0x24d0
  Read of size 1 at addr ffff888118130552 by task isotp_ns_uaf/578
   can_rcv_filter+0x4af/0x8c0
   can_receive+0x28d/0x3c0
   can_rcv+0x2a9/0x310
   __netif_receive_skb_one_core+0x21a/0x260
   process_backlog+0x210/0x760

Besides this, the lists of a device are protected by the rcvlists_lock
of the namespace that is passed in. Callers which pass dev_net(dev) read
it at different times, so the same lists may be modified under the locks
of different namespaces while the device is moved.

Taking RTNL in these release paths is no option: raw_bind(),
raw_setsockopt() and raw_release() already hold RTNL while adding and
removing up to CAN_RAW_FILTER_MAX filters per socket, which unprivileged
users can trigger repeatedly and which makes RTNL a global bottleneck.

Instead fix the root cause and add a spinlock to struct
can_dev_rcv_lists, which protects the receive lists of a CAN device or
the 'any' CAN device lists of a namespace. It is initialized in
can_set_ml_priv(), which is used by all CAN network devices. With this,
can_rx_unregister() finds the subscription independently of the
current namespace of the device. The protocols keep the device valid
with their tracked references. The per-netns rcvlists_lock only protects
the receive list statistics anymore, and CAN_RAW, CAN_BCM and CAN_ISOTP
pass the namespace that has been used for can_rx_register().

So isotp_release() and bcm_release() now remove their filters correctly
without RTNL, and raw_release(), raw_setsockopt(), raw_bind() and
isotp_bind() do not need RTNL anymore and add and remove their filters
under lock_sock(). To serialize bind() with NETDEV_UNREGISTER, bind()
publishes the device inside the RCU section of its lookup, and
raw_notify() and isotp_notify() recheck the bound device under lock_sock().
As RTNL does not keep NETDEV_DOWN out of bind() anymore, bind() checks
IFF_UP after publishing the bound device, with a barrier pair against
raw_notify() and isotp_notify(), so a down transition during bind() is
still reported with ENETDOWN.
title: can: protect the receive lists with a per-device lock

desc:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

can: replace ARPHRD_CAN type checks with can_get_ml_priv()

Commit 4e096a18867a ("net: introduce CAN specific pointer in the struct
net_device") introduced an explicit way to assign the midlayer private
pointer (dev->ml_priv) to named users like ML_PRIV_CAN. A valid pointer
returned by can_get_ml_priv() therefore identifies a real CAN device.

The referenced commit only converted the j1939 and proc code to this
check, while the other parts of the CAN subsystem still rely on
dev->type == ARPHRD_CAN.

The TUNSETLINK ioctl allows a down TUN/TAP device to set its hardware
type to ARPHRD_CAN while dev->ml_priv remains NULL. Such a repurposed
netdevice passes the ARPHRD_CAN checks.

Commit 8aa59e355949 ("can: af_can: fix NULL pointer dereference in
can_rx_register()") already made can_rx_register() reject such devices.
But can_rx_unregister() still only checks dev->type and dereferences
the NULL ml_priv when it walks the receive lists of the device.

CAN_ISOTP reaches this path: isotp_bind() ignores the return values of
can_rx_register() and binds the socket anyway. When the socket is
released or the device is unregistered, isotp_release() and
isotp_notify() remove the filters that have never been registered and
trigger the NULL pointer dereference in can_rx_unregister(). This only
requires owning a TUN/TAP device or CAP_NET_ADMIN in an unprivileged
user namespace.

Convert the remaining ARPHRD_CAN checks in af_can, bcm, gw, isotp and
raw to can_get_ml_priv().
title: can: replace ARPHRD_CAN type checks with can_get_ml_priv()

desc:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

mm/gup: fix clearing folios in memfd_pin_folios()

memfd_pin_folios() pins folios obtained directly from the page cache
without checking whether they are uptodate. However, shmem fallocate()
can leave newly allocated folios uncleared and not uptodate. Callers
such as udmabuf can then expose uninitialized memory to userspace.

Clear non-uptodate folios and mark them uptodate under the folio lock
before returning them to the caller.

Fix generated by an LLM and sent by Chris Mason in private.

[ david: simplify description and comment ]
title: mm/gup: fix clearing folios in memfd_pin_folios()

desc:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

mm/gup: recheck the PUD under PTL in follow_pud_mask()

follow_pud_mask() reads the PUD without a lock. If it is a leaf, it takes
the lock and calls follow_huge_pud(), which reads the entry again, but
only tests whether it is present.

A leaf can be zapped concurrently and a page fault can fill the empty
entry with a page table.

This currently only applies when device-dax makes use of PUD entries,
and the fault after e.g., MADV_DONTNEED would find THPs to be disabled.

That requires a sequence like

1) Fault in the PUD
2) Disable THP
3) Have GUP race against concurrent MADV_DONTNEED + refault

Which is rather unlikely to happen in practice, which is why we never
received a report about such a problem.

Before commit 1b1676180246 ("mm/gup: handle huge pud for
follow_pud_mask()"), we performed that check in follow_devmap_pud() by
testing for pud_devmap().

Let's fix it by just structuring follow_pud_mask() similar to
follow_pmd_mask(), minus protnone stuff that does not apply and minus
FOLL_SPLIT_PMD handling. That makes it much easier to spot any such
inconsistencies.

Perform the pud_bad() check early in follow_pmd_mask() and just forward
the PUD value. We can drop the pud_present() check in follow_huge_pud(),
just like we have in follow_huge_pmd().

Even though we are performing more changes than strictly necessary, the
fix should be easy to backport.
title: mm/gup: recheck the PUD under PTL in follow_pud_mask()

desc:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

mm/khugepaged: preserve dirty bits when collapsing PTE-mapped THPs

try_collapse_pte_mapped_thp() clears PTEs without transferring their dirty
bits to the folio. A shmem read fault can map a clean folio writable, so
a later store only dirties the PTE. Losing that dirty bit allows reclaim
to discard modified data.

The assumption that regular files are read-only is also obsolete since
commit 1b6444331bebb ("mm/khugepaged: enable clean pagecache folio collapse
for writable files"). In any case, transferring PTE dirty bits to the folio
when removing mappings (and while the folio is still mapped) is the right
thing to do.

Use get_and_clear_ptes() to collect the dirty bits and mark the folio
dirty before unmapping it. Update the comment.

This was reproduced with shmem using MADV_COLLAPSE followed by
MADV_PAGEOUT.

Fix generated by an LLM and sent by Chris Mason in private.

[ david: adjust comment; simplify description; cover file-thp as well ]
title: mm/khugepaged: preserve dirty bits when collapsing PTE-mapped THPs

desc:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

mm/khugepaged: fix PMD table lock leak in try_collapse_pte_mapped_thp()

For a private mapping with userfaultfd, try_collapse_pte_mapped_thp()
takes the PMD table lock before it maps the page table for the second time.
If that (pte_offset_map_rw_nolock) fails, because the page table vanished
in the meantime due to concurrent page table reclaim, it leaves through
the abort label, where the PMD table lock is unlocked if it differs from
PTE table lock.

In case the PMD table lock and the PTE table lock match, which is the
case without CONFIG_SPLIT_PTE_PTLOCKS after pte_offset_map_rw_nolock()
failed, we miss to unlock the PMD table.

To fix it, forget the PTE table lock when we unmap+unlock the PTE table.

Fix generated by an LLM and sent by Josef Bacik in private.

[ david: move the ptl = NULL handling; rewrite description, drop wrong comments ]
title: mm/khugepaged: fix PMD table lock leak in try_collapse_pte_mapped_thp()

desc:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

mm/userfaultfd: write-lock the VMA before waking waiters when unregistering

userfaultfd_unregister() wakes pending missing faults before clearing the
VMA's userfaultfd registration. With per-VMA fault locking, holding
mmap_lock for write does not prevent another fault from queuing after
the wakeup but before userfaultfd_clear_vma() write-locks the VMA. That
waiter can then remain asleep indefinitely.

Call vma_start_write() before waking waiters. Existing fault handlers
queue themselves before dropping the VMA read lock, and new readers are
excluded until mmap_write_unlock().
title: mm/userfaultfd: write-lock the VMA before waking waiters when unregistering

desc:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

mm/gup: check for overflow when converting nr_pages to bytes in GUP-fast

The overflow check in gup_fast_fallback() only covers the addition to
start. The preceding nr_pages << PAGE_SHIFT can already have truncated
the length on 32bit.
